newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan port workers begin 24-hour strike.
newsitem.headline: Japan port workers begin 24-hour strike.

text.p: Workers from two Japanese port unions started a 24-hour nationwide strike at 8 a.m. on Wednesday (2300 GMT on Tuesday) to protest against a U.S. decision to impose a $100,000 surcharge on Japanese ships calling at U.S. ports, union officials said.
They said it was the first time in 10 years port workers had staged a strike involving major Japanese ports.
Two port workers unions, the National Council of Dock Workers' Unions and the Japan Confederation of Port and Transport Workers' Unions, are striking at major ports, including Yokohama and Kobe.
All loading and unloading of ships at about 50 ports nationwide has stopped as a result of the strike, union members said.

They said the strike was to protest against the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission's (FMC) decision to impose sanctions on Japanese ships calling at U.S. ports, and also to call for better working conditions.
The FMC said the sanctions, to go into effect on April 14, would be imposed in retaliation of what it termed unfair Japanese port practices.

Japanese shipping company officials have expressed fears that the strike will make it more difficult to avert the U.S. sanctions, which could cost the Japanese shipping industry five billion yen ($41.3 million) a year.
Talks held last week in Washington between U.S. and Japanese officials failed to narrow their differences, a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.
